title: [Pulumi] AI infrastructure on tap with the Pulumi AICR provider
summary: Recently, some members of the Pulumi team spent time in San Francisco attending the CoreWeave: Fully Connected 2026 conference, where we had a chance to talk to everyone from solo developers to engineering leaders at Fortune 500 organizations and learn more about how they are building with AI. A frequent topic of conversation was open weight models and self-hosted inference. Whether AI is integrated into your platform, your product, or your productivity pipelines, rising token costs have decision makers everywhere giving open weight models a closer look, in exchange for the promise of tighter control over spend and greater domain expertise. If you are actively exploring the space or building with AI yourself, you may already have seen the challenges that come with serving inference at scale: Model stability and reliability can differ (sometimes dramatically) across hardware architectures and at different traffic volumes. Model performance and throughput can change depending on your workload type or model configuration. Cost differences and commitments across providers can make tracking spend challenging. Supply constraints and capacity shortages mean teams can’t source hardware when they need it most. Many teams naturally gravitate toward multicloud strategies that combine hyperscalers with specialized GPU clouds as a way of balancing spend, performance, and reliability. One thing we’ve seen is that developers everywhere are choosing Pulumi to help them navigate the fragmented hardware ecosystem and maintain consistent environments, even when the provider is different. As part of our ongoing commitment to building better tools for builders, we’re excited to announce the Pulumi NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) provider to help make your ideal self-hosted AI infrastructure available on demand. The Pulumi AICR provider lets you spin up workload-specific training and inference endpoints as you need them, configured with pre-validated recipes to match your workload with the right hardware across a number of cloud-based GPU providers. AI performance-engineering team as code Deploying a cluster of GPU nodes as a production AI platform is a complex and time-consuming exercise that often requires specialized expertise. NVIDIA’s AICR offers a collection of validated GPU infrastructure recipes for various cloud providers. By building a provider around AICR, Pulumi offers an efficient and reliable way to manage your GPU clusters, dramatically shortening time to first token. In addition to bundling a complex technology stack, Pulumi makes it simple to deploy with minimal verbosity. pulumi preview shows every component the recipe expands into (namespaces, operators, schedulers, metrics, training runtime) before anything is applied. pulumi up then deploys them as children of a single resource, with a full day-2 lifecycle: diff, update, drift detection, and destroy. This short Python snippet shows how easy it is to use AICR to deploy a simple pre-validated inference endpoint without wasting time or resources on guess-and-check configuration, so you can get started serving production traffic immediately. import pulumi import pulumi_labs_nvidia_aicr as aicr config = pulumi.Config() service = config.get("service") or "lke" accelerator = config.get("accelerator") or "rtx-pro-6000" # The CoreWeave Kubernetes Service (CKS) kubeconfig is a plain token config downloaded # from the CoreWeave console and placed in the same directory as this script (gitignored). with open("kubeconfig.yaml") as f: kubeconfig = f.read() gpu_stack = aicr.ClusterStack("nvidia-aicr", kubeconfig=pulumi.Output.secret(kubeconfig), accelerator=accelerator, service=service, intent="inference", nodes=2, skip_components=, skip_await=True, ) Deploying an inference endpoint to CoreWeave with the Pulumi NVIDIA AICR provider Behind the scenes, the recipe resolves the code into the full list of Kubernetes components. Recipes are tested and validated by NVIDIA across a broad matrix of both hardware (EKS, GKE, and AKS; A100 through GB200; Ubuntu, RHEL, COS, and Talos; Kubeflow, NIM, Dynamo, Slurm, and Run:ai) and cloud provider permutations. Because AICR is open source, the SDK lends itself to configuration by new providers, giving you a future-forward inference solution that performs in all of the areas that count: Deployment: does the running cluster match the recipe? Operator health, GPU visibility via nvidia-smi, and metrics flowing. Conformance: dynamic resource allocation, gang scheduling, and job-level networking behave as required. Performance: NCCL all-reduce bandwidth for training; model throughput and latency for inference. Interested in learning more about how Pulumi can help you scale your AI infrastructure? title: [Microsoft Azure] Azure Cloud HSM Hardware Audit Logging: Verifiable audit trails for security and compliance
summary: Organizations running regulated and security-sensitive workloads need trusted evidence of which authenticated users performed management operations on their hardware security modules (HSMs), what actions they took, and when. Today, we are announcing Hardware Audit Logging for Azure Cloud HSM, which collects audit records generated by the HSM itself for supported management operations. Security, compliance, and operations teams can use this hardware-originated evidence for monitoring, compliance reporting, and forensic investigations. Learn more about Azure Cloud HSM Why hardware-generated audit evidence matters HSMs protect some of an organization’s most sensitive cryptographic assets. The security of those assets depends not only on how keys are generated and protected, but also on how the HSM is configured and administered over time. Authentication events, user changes, policy updates, backup operations, and key lifecycle activity can all be important when teams investigate an incident, validate operational controls, or prepare evidence for an audit. Traditional platform and application logs remain valuable, but regulated organizations often want evidence that originates as close as possible to the protected cryptographic boundary. By sourcing audit information directly from the HSM, Azure Cloud HSM provides records tied to the device performing the protected operations. This gives customers an additional layer of evidence for understanding administrative activity and validating the records incorporated into their monitoring and compliance processes. Monitor HSM management operations with hardware-generated audit logs Hardware Audit Logging captures a broad range of HSM management activities, including: User authentication and session events. User and administrator management. Policy and configuration changes. Key lifecycle operations. Backup and restore activities. Together, these events help organizations build a more complete view of how the HSM is being operated. Security teams can examine authentication and administrative activity, compliance teams can use the records as evidence for control assessments, and operations teams can investigate configuration or lifecycle changes that may affect a protected workload. Independent, end-to-end audit verification Customers can access human-readable audit records, the corresponding HSM-signed binary audit data, signatures, and HSM certificates needed to independently verify the authenticity and integrity of signed audit batches. This customer-controlled verification path helps connect the records used in monitoring and reporting back to the signed evidence produced by the HSM. This approach is important because auditability is not only about collecting readable events. It is also about establishing confidence in where the records came from and whether the signed audit batches remain intact. Maintain consistent audit coverage for supported management activity Audit logging is enabled as an immutable HSM partition policy. This design helps maintain consistent coverage of supported management activity and reduces the risk that logging could be disabled as part of routine HSM administration. For organizations that separate cryptographic administration, security monitoring, and compliance responsibilities, continuous hardware-originated logging can support clearer oversight across those functions. The capability is designed to complement an organization’s existing governance model. Customers remain responsible for configuring access to their monitoring environment, defining retention requirements, establishing alerting and review processes, and determining how audit evidence should be used within their control framework. Hardware Audit Logging provides the HSM-originated records and verification materials that those processes can use. Integrate HSM audit data into security operations Hardware Audit Logging is designed for organizations with stringent compliance and security requirements, including financial services, payment processing, government, critical infrastructure, and other highly regulated industries. These organizations may need to demonstrate that sensitive cryptographic systems are administered through controlled processes and that important management activities can be reviewed after the fact. Audit events are delivered to Azure Monitor Log Analytics, enabling customers to incorporate HSM management activity into broader monitoring, investigation, and security operations workflows, including Microsoft Sentinel. Centralizing these events alongside other relevant operational and security data can help teams correlate HSM activity with events elsewhere in the environment, apply queries and analytics, and support established investigation and reporting workflows. For example, a security operations team may want to review unexpected authentication activity, an administrator change, or a policy update in the context of related Azure activity. A compliance team may need evidence that privileged management operations were logged during a defined assessment period. An incident response team may need to reconstruct the sequence of HSM management events surrounding a security investigation. Hardware-originated audit records provide an important source for each of these scenarios. Strengthen HSM auditability with verifiable evidence Azure Cloud HSM provides more than log visibility. Readable audit records support day-to-day operations. It also provides HSM-signed binary evidence, signatures, certificates, and verification utilities behind those records, which lead to an independent way to trace each record back to the HSM that signed it. It also allows for keeping that evidence outside the logging workflow and checking it cryptographically whenever an audit or investigation calls for it, instead of relying only on delivered text records. Teams get an audit trail they can verify for the workloads that matter most. What does Azure Cloud HSM Hardware Audit Logging provide It provides hardware-generated records for supported HSM management operations, sends audit events to Azure Monitor Log Analytics, and gives customers signed binary audit data and verification materials for independent validation. Azure Cloud HSM Hardware Audit Logging availability Hardware Audit Logging is rolling out across Azure Cloud HSM public regions and is automatically enabled for newly provisioned Azure Cloud HSM resources where the feature is available. Customers should review current Azure Cloud HSM regional availability and product documentation for the latest availability details and configuration guidance. Review the resources below to learn about Azure Cloud HSM, configure operation audit logs, and confirm regional availability. title: [Docker] Docker Sandboxes vs. Containers: Choosing the Right Isolation for AI Agents
summary: If you’ve used Docker for a while, “Docker Sandboxes” might read as “a container with an AI agent inside.” Containers have been the unit of nearly everything Docker ships for over a decade, and a sandbox might sound like one more way to package a workload. They’re actually different technologies. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel with everything else on the machine. Docker Sandboxes are dedicated microVMs with their own Linux kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine, built for autonomous coding agents that need a whole development machine to work in. A sandbox can run containers, which is part of why the two are easy to conflate. In his WeAreDevelopers keynote, Docker President Mark Cavage said containers are doing exactly the job they were designed to do, but we’re asking them to do a different job. Containers were built to isolate applications, which they still do well. But a coding agent is an actor: it makes decisions and operates on your systems the way a developer uses a laptop. It clones repositories, installs packages, starts databases, builds images, and tries again for hours. It can also act on instructions from files, web pages, and tool output that nobody reviewed. That different job needs a different boundary, and where that boundary sits determines how far an agent’s mistake can travel. This post covers how Docker Sandboxes and containers isolate workloads, what changes beyond the kernel, what a sandbox costs you in setup, and how to pick. Key takeaways A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine. Containers stay the right choice for packaged applications, CI jobs, and short-lived execution. Docker Sandboxes fit autonomous agents that need sudo, a private Docker Engine, long-lived state, and host-enforced network and credential controls. Containers can be part of an agent’s containment, and a sandbox can run them. Sandbox the agent, containerize the application it works on. What is a container? A container is a process, or a group of processes, running on the host with its own view of the filesystem, process tree, and network. Linux namespaces provide that view, and cgroups meter CPU, memory, and I/O. Every container on the machine also shares the host kernel, which is why containers start quickly, pack densely, and carry so little overhead. This design has more than a decade of tooling behind it. Compose, Kubernetes, OCI registries, image scanners, and nearly every CI system treat the container as the common primitive. If the job is to run a service, execute a code snippet, process one request, or run an evaluation and disappear, a container is usually the obvious pick, and it will stay that way. ⓘ Containers share one kernel, even inside a VM. On macOS and Windows, Docker Desktop runs your Linux containers inside a virtual machine, which keeps them off your host operating system. Every container in that VM still shares its single kernel, so the isolation between one container and the next is unchanged. What are Docker Sandboxes? Docker Sandboxes run an AI coding agent inside a microVM that has its own Linux kernel, its own filesystem and network stack, and a private Docker Engine. The agent gets sudo inside the isolated environment. It can install packages, run services, build images, and bring up an entire Compose application without reaching the host Docker daemon, the host filesystem outside its workspace, or other sandboxes on the same machine. Getting one running takes a single command, using sbx, the Docker Sandboxes CLI: sbx run claude That creates the sandbox and starts the agent. You can stop it, resume it, and come back to everything the agent installed until you remove the sandbox. Why do coding agents need a full machine? Coding agents need a full machine because their sessions build up state over hours and they act on unvetted instructions. A container is built for a process with a known set of dependencies, and an agent’s work doesn’t fit that shape. An agent needs the authority of a whole machine and a boundary designed for one. The capabilities that make an agent useful, such as running code, installing packages, and reaching the network, are the same ones that wear at the walls around it. An agent probes the edges of its environment because the job requires changing that environment. Agents accumulate state for hours A coding agent’s session looks like a developer’s afternoon. It clones a repository, installs packages, starts PostgreSQL, runs migrations, builds images, launches the app with Compose, reads the logs, changes the code, and tries again. That loop can run for hours, and each step depends on what the previous one left behind. A container is designed to be rebuilt from an image and a few explicit volumes. The packages, databases, and build output an agent creates outside those volumes are lost when the container is recreated. That’s less than ideal for a session where every step builds on the last. Box by ASCII describes this distinction neatly: “It uses the sandbox the way a developer uses a laptop, so the sandbox has to behave like one.” Agents act on untrusted instructions The program deciding which command to run is probabilistic, and it can read instructions from many places at once, including source files, issue descriptions, web pages, package metadata, and MCP tool output. Some of that input is untrusted, and a malicious instruction planted in a README or a tool description can steer the agent on purpose. The code it generates may also be wrong or actively hostile. We’ve already seen an agent that deleted a production database after misreading its task. Once the agent is running unattended in YOLO mode, there’s no permission prompt left to catch it. A workload with that much authority and that little predictability needs a boundary designed for it. Put these facts together and you get the reason why we built Docker Sandboxes. An autonomous coding agent needs machine-shaped capabilities without access to everything on the developer’s machine, which comes down to four things: Containment: a boundary the model can’t rewrite Control: observability into what the agent is doing and the ability to stop it Choice: the freedom to swap agents, models, and tools without rebuilding the setup Capacity: a setup other developers can reproduce and scale past one machine. The next sections show what each looks like, starting with containment. Containment: How isolation differs between containers and Docker Sandboxes The short version is that a container’s boundary is the host kernel it shares, and Docker Sandboxes have a hypervisor boundary around a kernel the agent has to itself. That one difference decides how far a compromise can travel, and it also settles the awkward question of how an agent could get access to Docker. This is where containers and containment part ways. A container can be part of containment, and often should be, but containment covers the whole environment around the agent. It starts with a boundary the model can’t rewrite, which is why Docker uses a microVM with its own kernel for autonomous agents. Shared kernel vs. dedicated kernel A container’s boundary is enforced by the kernel it shares, so escaping it requires a kernel exploit or a side-channel attack. Those aren’t everyday finds. Past that bar, though, sits the entire host kernel, every other process on the machine, and any credentials mounted alongside them. ⓘ This scenario is specific to Linux environments. On Docker Desktop (macOS and Windows), the shared kernel is the Docker Desktop VM’s kernel, not the host kernel, so an escape would land in that VM rather than the operating system. Docker Sandboxes give the agent its own kernel behind a hypervisor boundary. If an agent escapes its container, it lands in a disposable microVM, and the host stays out of reach. And you can delete the sandbox and start another. Each agent also gets its own microVM, so two agents running on the same machine can’t reach each other’s sandboxes either. However, the agent can still reach whatever you chose to share with it, including the workspace, allowed network destinations, MCP servers, and skills. The Docker socket problem Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container is the long-standing way to give it Docker access, and it turns up in Compose setups, CI pipelines, and observability tools. It also hands the container control of the host Docker daemon, which Docker limits to trusted users because it can mount host paths and start privileged containers. An agent doesn’t need an exploit to use that. Put one in a container started with the socket mounted, and it probes its surroundings, works out that it’s in a container, and finds the hole in the configuration. In Mark’s keynote demo, that was enough for an agent to reach a secrets file on the host with no zero-day involved. The socket is one hole among several, and agents find them because probing their environment is part of the work. Docker-in-Docker, mounted credentials, and broad host mounts are others. Containers were built to isolate an application that behaves as configured. But an agent keeps testing that configuration, so if there’s a gap, it’s likely to find it. Where the microVM boundary goes Docker Sandboxes put the missing boundary in the right place. The agent talks to a private Docker Engine inside the guest. It can build images, run Testcontainers, and start a whole Compose stack, and the host daemon and its socket stay outside the microVM the entire time. Containers keep doing what they do best, inside a boundary the agent can’t widen. Let’s say you ask an agent running inside Docker Sandboxes to find a secrets file on the host. It’ll find a Docker socket, try to use it to mount host paths and start privileged containers, but won’t reach the host. A microVM can give it a much stronger trust boundary than a container. The architecture behind Docker Sandboxes goes deeper on why a microVM was the right shape for this. Control: What you can see and stop beyond the kernel Containment draws the boundary. Control is what you can see and stop inside it: what the agent is allowed to reach, and the ability to block it when it heads somewhere it shouldn’t. In a sandbox, those controls are enforced by the host, outside the agent’s reach, so the agent can’t switch them off or reason its way around them. Outbound traffic, credentials, and organization-wide policy all work this way. Control also means knowing what the agent can still touch, because a microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it. Agent in a standard container Agent in Docker Sandboxes Kernel Shares the host kernel Runs its own Linux kernel in a microVM Docker Needs the host socket or a nested daemon Uses a private Docker Engine inside the microVM Workspace Sees the host paths you mount Uses a direct read-write mount or an in-VM private clone Network Uses the container network and whatever controls its operator supplies Sends outbound traffic through a host proxy with deny-by-default policy Credentials Commonly receives environment variables, files, or mounted sockets Uses host-side credential injection for supported HTTP services State Usually rebuilt from an image and explicit volumes Keeps packages, images, containers, and agent history until sbx rm Orchestration Fits Compose, Kubernetes, and most CI systems Uses the sbx lifecycle and experimental environment files The host enforces the controls These controls hold because they run outside the agent process. A rule the agent can reach is a rule it can work around, so the rules that matter live on the host. Outbound traffic goes through a host-side proxy with a deny-by-default policy, which means a destination the agent wants stays blocked until someone adds it to the list. Credentials follow the same logic. For supported HTTP services, the proxy injects them into outbound requests, so the agent can use a credential without the raw value ever entering the VM. When one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance can move network, filesystem, and MCP policy into organization-wide controls. What the agent can still reach A microVM can’t hide what you choose to share with it, so the shared parts deserve the most attention. The workspace is the largest of them. It’s mounted read-write by default, so the agent can edit or delete files in your project. Clone mode gives the agent a private in-VM clone to work in, which protects the host working tree, though the original repository stays readable inside the sandbox. MCP servers and skills are shared too. A local stdio MCP server runs on the host and shared agent skills use a host-side store, so the agent’s reach extends to both. So whichever mode you pick, be sure to read the diff before you run modified code. Choice and capacity: What Docker Sandboxes cost you in setup Docker Sandboxes may cost some configuration and a supported hypervisor. But Kits and environment files account for the configuration, and they’re also where you get choice over agents and tools and the capacity to reproduce a setup across a team. Kits and environment files Kits make setup repeatable by packaging tools, files, commands, network rules, credentials, and agent instructions. They’re published for different agents, tools, and IDEs, so you can swap what runs inside the sandbox without rebuilding the environment around it. An sbxenv.yaml file records one project’s sandbox configuration, and committing it to the repo lets a teammate recreate the same sandbox with one command, so every developer works from the same setup. (Kits are in early access and environment files are experimental, so plan for changes to both.) The host-enforced controls take some setup too. Network policy requires someone to decide which destinations belong in the workflow, credential mediation adds service bindings and approved domains, and clone mode adds a fetch step before changes land in the host repository. Hypervisor and resource requirements Running a sandbox takes more from your machine than running a container does. It needs a supported hypervisor, which today means Apple silicon on macOS 14 or later, Windows Hypervisor Platform, or KVM on supported Ubuntu systems, and running inside another VM requires nested virtualization. The separate kernel and Docker Engine also consume more memory and disk than one additional container would. If your machine is the limiting factor, Docker Cloud Sandboxes run the same microVM isolation on Docker-managed compute, and one command moves a sandbox between your laptop and the cloud. Local and cloud sandboxes keep separate secrets and network policies. How do you choose between a container and Docker Sandboxes? Choose a container when you control the code and its dependencies, and choose Docker Sandboxes when the workload generates or fetches code at runtime and needs its own boundary. Reach for a container when Reach for Docker Sandboxes when You control the code and its dependencies The workload generates or fetches code at runtime Execution is short-lived and rebuilt from an image The session accumulates state for hours The workload doesn’t need Docker, or runs in CI that already provides it The workload needs its own Docker Engine with no path to the host socket You want maximum density and a fit with Compose or Kubernetes You need host-enforced network and credential policy the workload can’t switch off The kernel boundary is enough for the code you’re running You want a hypervisor between the workload and your kernel If any of the signals below apply to your project, you should start with Docker Sandboxes. The agent runs unattended, or its permission prompts are auto-approved The agent needs to build images or run Compose or Testcontainers The agent reads input you didn’t write, such as issues, web pages, package metadata, or MCP output The agent requires API keys you don’t want inside its environment The session lasts longer than a single task Start with sbx run claude. Add clone mode, kits, network policy, credential mediation, and organization governance as your workflow grows. Sandbox the agent, containerize the application Containers aren’t going anywhere. For services, CI jobs, and anything you package to ship, they draw the right boundary, and the ecosystem around them is the reason they’ll keep doing that work. A coding agent needs more than a container to be trusted with real work. It needs containment, meaning a boundary the model can’t rewrite, controls it can’t reason its way around, and the freedom to choose its tools and scale its setup. Docker Sandboxes provide that containment in a microVM that can still run your containers. The boundary is also what lets the agent move faster. With it in place, you can stop approving every command and let the agent get to work. You can have a sandbox running with one command. Start with sbx run claude and the Docker Sandboxes quickstart. Once one developer’s setup needs to become a team standard, Docker AI Governance extends the same controls across your organization. Frequently asked questions Are Docker Sandboxes just containers? No. A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel. Docker Sandboxes are microVMs with their own kernel, filesystem, network, and Docker Engine. A sandbox can run containers, which is why the two are easy to confuse. Can I run Docker inside Docker Sandboxes? Yes. Each sandbox has a private Docker Engine, so the agent can build images, run Testcontainers, and start Compose applications without the host socket or Docker-in-Docker. Do Docker Sandboxes replace containers? No. Containers remain the right tool for packaged applications, CI jobs, and short-lived execution. Sandboxes add a stronger boundary for autonomous agents, and containers keep running inside them. What’s the difference between a container and containment? A container isolates a workload. Containment involves the whole environment around an agent: the boundary it runs in, what it can reach, which tools it uses, and how you reproduce it. A container can be part of containment, and Docker Sandboxes add the microVM boundary an autonomous agent needs. What does an AI agent need from its environment? Docker describes four requirements: containment (a boundary the model can’t rewrite), control (visibility into what the agent is doing and the ability to stop it), choice (swapping models, agents, and tools without rebuilding), and capacity (a setup other developers can reproduce and scale past one machine). What do I need to run Docker Sandboxes? A supported hypervisor, which means Apple silicon on macOS 14 or later, Windows Hypervisor Platform, or KVM on supported Ubuntu systems. Running inside another VM requires nested virtualization.

title: [CNCF] OpenKruise Agents v0.6.0: Leaping ahead in agent Sandbox security and automation
summary: About OpenKruise Agents OpenKruise Agents is a sub-project of OpenKruise, the CNCF open-source application automation and workload orchestration project. It provides full lifecycle management for Agent Sandboxes running at scale on Kubernetes, together with a complete runtime environment covering networking, storage, and identity. OpenKruise Agents exposes both Kubernetes and E2B interfaces, so infrastructure teams, platform teams, and AI algorithm engineers can all operate sandboxes conveniently. The v0.3.0 release answered one question: once a Sandbox is handed to an Agent, how do you upgrade it, resize it, and account for it. Its roadmap closed with two promises — network governance through TrafficPolicy / SecurityProfile, and a security identity integration that keeps platform credentials out of Agent code. OpenKruise Agents v0.6.0 delivers both, and adds the operational machinery around them: 283 merged pull requests and 27 new contributors since v0.3.0. This post covers four capabilities in depth: L4 and L7 network access control plus token management — destination reachability, per-request inspection, MCP tool-level ACLs, and credential injection from Kubernetes Secrets; SandboxUpdateOps with CheckpointRestore and paused-instance upgrades — batch-upgrade a hibernated fleet without waking it by hand, and without losing the filesystem; PoolAutoscaler — declarative warm pool capacity with watermarks and cron schedules; Automatic pause and resume — probe-driven idle detection, scheduled wake, and wake-on-traffic, so idle Sandboxes stop consuming CPU. Together these deliver three kinds of customer value: security hardening, operational capability, and cost optimization. The post is organized in three parts: the architecture changes that made them possible, a deep dive into the four capabilities, and the value summary and roadmap. Part One: What Changed in the Architecture If v0.3.0 was a workload layer, v0.6.0 is a workload layer with its own data plane. Traffic inspection, policy distribution, and identity all became first-class components rather than external add-ons. The overall architecture: OpenKruise Agents v0.6.0 overall architecture From four components to six. v0.6.0 adds traffic-control-plane and traffic-proxy: ComponentRole in v0.6.0sandbox-managerStateless backend serving the E2B-compatible northbound API; owns sandbox lifecycle, quota, and route & traffic-token orchestrationsandbox-controllerReconciles Sandbox, SandboxSet, SandboxClaim and warm pools; hosts admission webhooks; drives the automatic pause/resume controllersandbox-gatewayData plane built on Envoy Go filters. The ingress gateway proxies user traffic (host/path routing, access tokens, wake-on-traffic); the egress gateway enforces policy-driven L7 egresstraffic-control-plane (new)istiod distributes xDS configuration to gateways and in-pod proxies; the Egress Policy Enforcer (EPE) applies L7 policy, MCP ACL, and token injection on egress trafficagent-runtimeSidecar providing E2B envd-compatible command, file, and port (49983) operationstraffic-proxy (new)Sidecar acting as the in-pod L4 enforcement point for egress traffic policies Two consequences are worth internalizing. First, egress is no longer the Pod’s own business — it is captured in-pod, routed through an egress gateway, and decided by a policy engine that sees the full request, not just the socket. Second, the ingress gateway can wake a sandbox, which is what makes wake-on-traffic possible without an external poller. what makes wake-on-traffic possible without an external poller. The CRD count doubled from 6 to 12, adding PoolAutoscaler, TrafficPolicy, GlobalTrafficPolicy, SecurityProfile, and GlobalSecurityProfile — a multi-tier control system spanning cluster, tenant, and sandbox scopes. Part Two: The Four Core Capabilities 2.1 Network Access Control and Token Management This is the largest change in the release. It answers three questions: what a Sandbox may access, who may access a Sandbox, and — the question most platforms get wrong — who actually holds the upstream API key. The data plane uses a two-stage traffic takeover, node-side L4 plus central L7, balancing performance and function: Sandbox application container -> traffic-proxy (in-pod L4 capture; Deny hits are blocked in place) -> egress gateway (central gateway chosen by egress routing) -> Envoy external processing (ext_proc) -> Egress Policy Enforcer decision (L7 / MCP ACL / credential injection) -> external service, or a blocked response L4 filtering completes node-side with very low latency; L7 deep inspection is centralized in the gateway for unified operations, observability, and security audit. The split is deliberate: L4 denials are dropped before traffic reaches the gateway, and L7 can never override an L4 denial. L4: is this destination reachable at all TrafficPolicy selects caller Pods and holds an ordered egress rule list; peers support fqdn, cidr, service, and workload. Three semantics matter more than the syntax: Once a policy selects a Pod, egress traffic matching no allow rule is denied — a policy is a whitelist once active; Rules with a missing peer field are skipped by the compiler and do not form a default deny — a typo in to silently weakens the policy; Always allow the cluster DNS Service, or every FQDN rule will look broken. apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: TrafficPolicy metadata: name: sandbox-egress spec: selector: matchLabels: app: traffic-sample egress: rules: - action: allow to: - service: {name: kube-dns, namespace: kube-system} - action: allow to: - fqdn: api.example.com - action: reject ports:  to: - cidr: 10.0.0.0/8 L7: what is this specific request allowed to do SecurityProfile matches HTTP requests and applies actions. block and bypass are terminating; mcpToolPolicy, headerManipulation, tokenTransformation, and audit are not. The highest-value use for Agent workloads is SSRF protection — prompt-injected code almost always tries internal services and cloud metadata endpoints: apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: GlobalSecurityProfile metadata: name: cluster-baseline spec: selector: matchLabels: {app: traffic-sample} priority: 50 # cluster baseline deliberately ordered before tenant profiles rules: - name: deny-metadata-endpoint match: - domains: - metadata.internal - "*.internal.company.com" actions: block: statusCode: 403 body: '{"error":"access to internal services is forbidden"}' MCP tool-level ACL When an Agent talks to an MCP Server, domain-level control is too coarse; the real risk is a specific tool. mcpToolPolicy governs only JSON-RPC tools/call and matches params.name exactly. Use defaultAction: deny for a whitelist. Credential injection: your API key never enters the Sandbox Credentials live in Kubernetes Secrets; the egress proxy resolves them per request and rewrites the outbound request as it leaves the cluster. Workloads and Agent code only ever see their own placeholder header. apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: SecurityProfile metadata: name: example-api-credentials namespace: agent-demo spec: selector: matchLabels: {app: agent} rules: - name: inject-example-api-key match: - domains:  schemes:  paths:  actions: tokenTransformation: type: ApiKey failStrategy: Block # fail closed when the credential is missing credentialRef: secret: name: example-api-credentials apiKey: targetHeaders: names:  value: template: "Bearer {{ .Token }}" Because resolution happens proxy-side, credentials never appear in Pod specs, environment variables, or Sandbox metadata, and rotating a Secret takes effect without restarting the Sandbox. Core performance metrics The traffic-control data plane is built around sandbox-gateway and has been validated at production scale. Reference gateway specifications (Alibaba Cloud ACS Agent Sandbox default deployment): MetricValue / specificationPer-replica instance size4 vCPU / 8 GiB (default)Default replicas3Per-replica ingress+egress bandwidth1.5 Gbit/sTheoretical throughput ceiling1.5 Gbit/s / 2 (bidirectional) / 8 ≈ 93.75 MB/sRecommended business traffic≈ 90 MB/s per replicaL4 filtering locationNode-side traffic-proxy, completed in kernel space with very low latencyMetrics endpointPort 9902 (Prometheus format)Tuning noteenvoy.concurrency must be adjusted together with resources.cpu Note: these are theoretical upper bounds, not committed service metrics. Observe request duration via the gateway log duration_ms field and watch for 502s or packet loss in production. In production at leading customers, this sandbox and traffic-control stack supports: MiniMax (MaxClaw): custom template pre-warming plus MicroVM for 20–40 ms instance provisioning, up to 15,000 sandboxes/minute of elastic supply. Kimi (Moonshot AI): tens of thousands of concurrent requests at peak with a hundred-thousand-Pod backend; minute-level thousand-node scale-out. Li Auto: MicroVM hardware isolation with fine-grained east-west and north-south traffic control; about 800 employees in daily use, planned to grow to tens or hundreds of thousands of Agents. Guardrails you must not skip. Controls cover only gateway-routed traffic; containers running as root or with NET_ADMIN / SYS_ADMIN can bypass in-pod ACLs. Combine these policies with Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, host firewalls, or cloud security groups — this is defense in depth, not a wall. 2.2 SandboxUpdateOps: CheckpointRestore and Paused-Instance Upgrades v0.3.0 offered a single mode, Recreate: destroy and rebuild the Pod, losing memory, IP, and the writable rootfs layer. v0.6.0 adds the two most-requested capabilities — a mode that preserves rootfs, and the ability to include paused Sandboxes in batch upgrades. ModeRootfsMemory / IPChange business imageRecreate (default)LostLost / changesSupportedCheckpointRestorePreserved (snapshot before, restore after)Lost / changesNot supported CheckpointRestore trades image flexibility for data continuity and is the standard way to roll sidecars such as agent-runtime or traffic-proxy: user data untouched, no backup scripts. The new stateFilter lets the controller wake each paused Sandbox, upgrade it, and re-pause it while `spec.paused` remains true — the fleet ends in the same shape it started, so one upgrade never quietly turns a hibernating pool into a bill. apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: SandboxUpdateOps metadata: name: upgrade-with-paused namespace: default spec: stateFilter: states:  # include paused instances in the upgrade selector: matchLabels: agents.kruise.io/sandbox-template: my-sandbox-pool updateStrategy: maxUnavailable: 10% patch: spec: containers: - name: sandbox image: my-registry/sandbox-image:v2 2.3 Warm Pool Autoscaling Warm pools are why OpenKruise Agents can claim a Sandbox in sub-second time — and why the platform bill keeps rising at night when nobody is using it. PoolAutoscaler turns pool capacity from “a cron job running kubectl scale” into a declarative policy: it rewrites SandboxSet.spec.replicas, providing watermark feedback based on available capacity plus time-driven cron overrides. apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: PoolAutoscaler metadata: name: sandbox-pool-scaler namespace: default spec: scaleTargetRef: {kind: SandboxSet, name: sandbox-pool} minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 50 capacityPolicy: targetAvailable: "50%" # keep half the capacity available to absorb claim bursts tolerance: "10%" scaleUp: {stabilizationWindowSeconds: 60} # scale up fast scaleDown: {stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300} # scale down slow cronPolicies: - name: weekday-peak timezone: Asia/Shanghai schedule: "30 8 * * 1-5" # scale up before the morning peak targetReplicas: 30 - name: weekday-offpeak timezone: Asia/Shanghai schedule: "0 20 * * 1-5" # scale down at night to save cost targetReplicas: 5 Asymmetric stabilization windows (fast scale-up, slow scale-down) are the correct default for warm pools: users feel shortages immediately and never notice slow scale-down. Cron triggers take priority and fire before the burst arrives. A complementary cost capability is in-place memory resize at claim time. A warm pool does not need to hold instances at peak business memory: the pool can warm at a small uniform size, and when a SandboxClaim claims an instance, an in-place resize adjusts the main container’s CPU/memory to what that task actually needs (in-place resize of a running Pod requires Kubernetes 1.33+; the SandboxInPlaceResourceResize feature gate is enabled by default). This sacrifices some delivery speed — an in-place resize is slightly slower than claiming an instance that already fits — but remains far faster than cold-starting a new Sandbox, and it sharply cuts warm pool holding cost: the pool holds one fleet of small instances instead of a large fleet per business size. 2.4 Automatic Pause and Resume To Kubernetes, a claimed Sandbox with an active session and one nobody has touched for four hours look identical. Automatic pause/resume makes that difference observable and acts on it. It is configured through two top-level SandboxSet fields, probes and autoPausePolicy, with three capabilities: Idle-driven pause: a probe (exec only) reports activity periodically; sustained idle beyond thresholdDuration pauses the Sandbox; Scheduled wake: for workloads with a timetable (e.g. daily knowledge organization at midnight, a weekly report on Friday afternoon), a probe prints the next activation time and the controller wakes the Sandbox ahead of it; Wake-on-traffic: the first request after pause wakes the Sandbox instead of failing — the key to making pause safe for user-facing scenarios. The following SandboxSet enables both idle pause and scheduled wake: apiVersion: agents.kruise.io/v1alpha1 kind: SandboxSet metadata: name: openclaw-sbs namespace: default spec: replicas: 4 probes: - name: Active containerName: sandbox periodSeconds: 30 timeoutSeconds: 5 exec: command: - sh - -c - | # Example only; define the idle state per your business. if openclaw sessions list --active 900 2>/dev/null | grep -q .; then echo "active" else echo "inactive" fi - name: Cron containerName: sandbox periodSeconds: 30 timeoutSeconds: 5 exec: command: - sh - -c - | # Example only: next run time of the earliest enabled task # (daily 00:00 knowledge organization, Friday 15:00 weekly report) NEXT_MS=$(openclaw cron list --json 2>/dev/null \ | jq -r ' | select(.enabled != false) | .nextRunAtMs] | map(select(. != null)) | sort | .') if  && ; then echo $((NEXT_MS / 1000)) # nextRunAtMs is milliseconds; divide by 1000 else echo "none" # no pending task: no wake schedule fi autoPausePolicy: pause: whenProbedIdleState: # idle-driven pause probe: Active messageRegex: "^inactive$" thresholdDuration: 10m # pause after 10 consecutive idle minutes resume: whenProbedScheduleTime: # scheduled wake probe: Cron timeFormat: unix leadTime: 5m # wake 5 minutes before the task template: spec: containers: - name: sandbox image: <YOUR_IMAGE> The Cron probe fetches the next scheduled task time every 30 seconds: the example filters enabled tasks from openclaw cron list, sorts by nextRunAtMs, takes the earliest (the nearer of the daily midnight knowledge organization and the Friday afternoon weekly report), and prints it as Unix seconds after dividing milliseconds by 1000; with no pending task it prints none and the controller creates no wake schedule. leadTime: 5m wakes the Sandbox 5 minutes before the task. Three behaviors are universal: requests must pass authentication (unauthorized requests return 401 and the Sandbox stays paused — wake-on-traffic is not an unauthenticated doorbell); a successful wake can accompany a failed request (the waking call may return 503; check Sandbox.status.phase and retry); a failed or timed-out probe never triggers pause or wake — the safe side. from e2b_code_interpreter import Sandbox sandbox = Sandbox.create( template="code-interpreter", timeout=600, lifecycle={"on_timeout": "pause", "auto_resume": True}, ) host = sandbox.get_host(3000) # first request triggers wake-on-traffic Part Three: Customer Value and Roadmap Value dimensionWhat v0.6.0 changesSecurity hardeningL4 whitelist + L7 request inspection + MCP tool whitelist + cluster-level baselines; credentials resolved proxy-side from Secrets and rotatable without restart; short-lived rotatable JWT traffic access tokensOperational capabilitystateFilter covers Running and Paused; CheckpointRestore preserves rootfs; PoolAutoscaler makes capacity declarative; automatic pause turns idle detection into a probeCost optimizationIdle Sandboxes pause on probe evidence and wake on schedule or first request; pools scale down at night and up before peaks; paused fleets still receive upgrades, avoiding data loss and needless wake cost Roadmap: community capability building. The next phase emphasizes co-building with other open-source communities rather than a closed in-house stack: Open-source checkpoint with the Kata community — based on the PodCheckpoint API introduced in Kubernetes 1.37, removing dependence on platform-specific snapshot backends; On-demand mounting for open-source storage — MinIO and similar storage mounted on demand through the existing on-demand mounting framework; Integration with open-source identity systems — for example Keycloak, so platform authentication reuses your existing identity provider. Getting Involved OpenKruise Agents is built entirely in the open. If you run Agent Sandboxes on Kubernetes, the fastest way to help shape the roadmap is to file an issue or join the community meeting. v0.6.0 is available on GitHub Releases and major image registries.
