title: [Docker] CNCF Score project improved its security posture by joining the Docker-Sponsored Open Source Program
summary: Score, a CNCF Sandbox project, recently joined the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program to strengthen the security of its container images and release pipeline. In this post, the Score maintainers share what we adopted (Docker Hub, Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, the Docker GitHub Builder, and OIDC connections), the results we measured, and how other open source projects, within the CNCF and beyond, can apply the same practices by default. The Opportunity In September 2025, the CNCF announced a partnership with Docker to expand infrastructure support for project maintainers through the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The partnership gives CNCF projects access to Docker’s security scanning tools, container registry, and best-practice resources at no cost. This aligned closely with the discussions held at the Maintainer Summit NA 2025 in Atlanta, which centered on increasing collaboration across CNCF projects and demonstrating security best practices. The Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program supports non-commercial open source projects with Docker tooling and infrastructure. Eligible projects receive: Verified Docker-Sponsored Open Source badge Removal of rate limits for developers Access to Docker Scout for software supply chain management Insights and analytics Repository logo Improved discoverability on Docker Hub Docker Hub Before: Score publishes different container images: the CLIs of score-compose, score-k8s, score-helm and score-radius; and the sample-score-app used for demos and testing. We previously published them in the GitHub Container Registry here. After: Through the DSOS Program, we now publish these images on Docker Hub, which increases their visibility and gives the community a verified, trusted source. All the container images are now available on Docker Hub. The program also provides usage analytics that show how the community uses these images. Here is an example: Docker Scout Before: As a CNCF project, Score follows the OpenSSF best practices. In addition, the OpenSSF Scorecard GitHub Action runs continuously. This was a solid foundation, but we had no dedicated security scanning tool in place. After: The DSOS Program gave us access to Docker Scout, which we now use in our pull requests and on our container registry (Docker Hub). This gives us clear visibility into the CVEs introduced or fixed by each pull request and release. The following GitHub Actions step uses docker/scout-action on every pull request to compare the image built from the PR branch with the one built from the main branch: - name: Docker Scout Comparison between main branch and current PR branch uses: docker/scout-action@v1 with: command: compare image: local://score-compose:pr-${{ github.event.number }} to: local://score-compose:main write-comment: true github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} organization: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} Here is an example of a comment posted by this docker/scout-action step in a recent Pull Request: The comment details the comparison between the two images (before versus after): size, packages updated, added or removed, CVEs introduced and resolved, and compliance with our policies in place (run as non-root, no critical CVEs, no packages with AGPL v3 licences). The analysis goes beyond the images themselves: it also covers the Go libraries and binaries they contain. The Docker Scout console also provides a single view of CVEs, packages, base images, and policies across all of our container images, which makes it easy to see what is used where, and in which version. Docker Hardened Images When Docker made Hardened Images freely available under Apache 2.0, we saw an opportunity to simplify our security posture while staying compatible with our existing Dockerfiles and workflows, even though we were already using multi-stage builds and distroless base images. Docker Hardened Images are minimal, security-focused container base images designed to reduce inherited risk in downstream projects. They are built and maintained with security and transparency as defaults, and offer: Minimal attack surface: Only required components are included. Non-root execution: Images run as non-root by default. Supply chain security: Includes published SBOMs and SLSA Level 3 build provenance. Active maintenance: Images are patched and rebuilt as vulnerabilities are disclosed. Open standards: All images are reproducible, open source, and licensed under Apache 2.0, making them compatible with CNCF governance and distribution models. The migration was straightforward. Take the score-radius CLI, which used a golang:alpine and a distroless images and now uses dhi.io/golang and dhi.io/static images. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal: In the associated PR here, image size dropped by 0.3 MB while the number of packages stayed the same and the CVE count remained at 0. We could have stayed with Debian, but chose to move to an Alpine base image (DHI provides the two options): The same applies to the NodeJS sample-score-app, which used nodejs on top of an alpine image and now uses a dhi.io/node image. The changes required in the Dockerfile were minimal: In the associated PR here, 22 packages were removed (including the package manager and the shell), along with 2 CVEs: Note: We were able to present a short walkthrough of our DHI integration during the CNCF webinar held on January 23, 2026, which accompanied the Docker Hardened Images announcement for CNCF projects. Docker GitHub Builder Although not directly part of the DSOS Program, we took the opportunity to adopt the new docker/github-builder GitHub reusable workflow to release our container images. This model provides a build pipeline maintained in the Docker organization, with a version-controlled BuildKit environment, multi-platform builds distributed across runners where beneficial, and signed SLSA provenance recording both the source commit and the builder identity. The trade-off is intentional. You retain control over when the build runs and which inputs it uses, while the build implementation itself lives in the Docker-maintained workflow rather than in per-repository job steps. Before, the GitHub Actions workflow to release our container images was using this sequence of actions: docker/setup-buildx-action docker/login-action docker/build-push-action cosign sign release-container-image: runs-on: ubuntu-latest permissions: id-token: write packages: write steps: - name: Set up Docker Buildx uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3 - name: Login to Docker Hub (docker.io) uses: docker/login-action@v4 with: registry: docker.io username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_RELEASE_TOKEN }} - name: Login to GitHub Container Registry uses: docker/login-action@v4 with: registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - name: Build and push docker image id: build-push-container uses: docker/build-push-action@v6 with: context: . platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 push: true provenance: mode=max sbom: true tags: | ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose:${{ github.ref_name }} ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose:latest docker.io/scorespec/score-compose:${{ github.ref_name }} docker.io/scorespec/score-compose:latest build-args: | "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" - name: Sign container image run: | cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose@${{ steps.build-push-container.outputs.digest }} cosign sign --yes scorespec/score-compose@${{ steps.build-push-container.outputs.digest }} After, this same workflow is now only using the reusable workflow docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml: release-container-image: uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1 permissions: contents: read id-token: write packages: write with: output: image push: true platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64 sbom: true cache: true context: . set-meta-labels: true set-meta-annotations: true build-args: | "VERSION=${{ github.ref_name }}" meta-images: | ghcr.io/score-spec/score-compose scorespec/score-compose meta-tags: | type=ref,event=tag latest registry-identities: | - type: dockerhub registry: docker.io username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} connection_id: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }} secrets: registry-auths: | - registry: ghcr.io username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} Docker GitHub Builder gives us a Docker-maintained build pipeline with signed SLSA provenance and SBOM attestations, helping consumers verify the builder identity and trace images back to their source commit. Signing uses GitHub OIDC, so we don’t need to manage long-lived signing keys. With caching enabled in our workflow, cache entries are also signed and verified before reuse, helping protect against cache poisoning. See the Docker GitHub Builder documentation for more information about its security model. The following command verifies the signature on the attestation manifest for the selected image platform: TAG=latest PLATFORM=amd64 SIGNED_DIGEST=$(crane manifest scorespec/score-compose:$TAG \ | jq -r --arg platformdigest \ "$(crane digest --platform linux/$PLATFORM scorespec/score-compose:$TAG)" \ '.manifests | select(.annotations == $platformdigest) | .digest') cosign verify \ --experimental-oci11 \ --new-bundle-format \ --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \ --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/docker/github-builder/\.github/workflows/build\.yml@.*$' \ scorespec/score-compose@$SIGNED_DIGEST OIDC Connections Most recently, with an update released on July 21, 2026, Docker introduced OIDC connections. This feature allows pulls and pushes to Docker Hub to use a short-lived token instead of a long-lived Organization Access Token (OAT). An OIDC connection establishes a trust relationship between Docker and a trusted third party, so you no longer need to maintain long-lived credentials. Docker exchanges short-lived tokens with the other vendor, which can grant fine-grained access to your Docker resources. Before: With docker/login-action: steps: - uses: docker/login-action@v4 with: username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_TOKEN }} Or with docker/github-builder: uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1 with: ... secrets: registry-auths: | - username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_HUB_TOKEN }} After: With docker/login-action: permissions: id-token: write steps: - uses: docker/login-action@v4 # v4.5.0+ env: DOCKERHUB_OIDC_CONNECTIONID: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }} with: username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} Or with docker/github-builder: uses: docker/github-builder/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1 # v1.15.0+ permissions: id-token: write with: ... registry-identities: | - type: dockerhub registry: docker.io username: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_ORG }} connection_id: ${{ vars.DOCKER_HUB_OIDC_CONNECTION_ID }} By replacing a static, long-lived token with a short-lived one and making it issued on a per-workflow basis, we removed a credential that could otherwise be stolen and misused. Wrapping Up Participating in the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program has been rewarding, and it has helped Score adopt a security-by-default foundation. Using Docker Scout, Docker Hardened Images, OIDC connections, and the Docker GitHub Builder has strengthened the security posture of our container images and brought broader benefits to the Score projects and repositories. If you maintain a CNCF project or any open source project, we encourage you to explore the Docker-Sponsored Open Source (DSOS) Program. The security improvements were measurable, and the onboarding process was straightforward. The full implementation across the Score repositories is tracked in GitHub issue #376. Attending KubeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City? Feel free to connect with the Score maintainers during the Maintainer Summit on Sunday, Nov 8th and at the Kiosk #P-17B on Thursday, Nov 12th between 10:15am and 2pm, you will see Score in actions with the new Score Labspace! You can also meet the Docker team at booth #141 in Hall C! Note: This work was completed after I joined Docker. It was, however, an initiative we wanted to pursue as CNCF project maintainers from the moment it was announced in September 2025, both to improve our security posture and to share what we learned with the broader community. We hope this post helps you strengthen the security of your own projects.

title: [Engineering at Meta] Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape
summary: The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty. For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next. Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty. Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities: Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks. Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them. Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work, especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward. AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs. AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options. Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else. Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors: “I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.” “Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.” When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help. The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows. Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does. Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. Among 156 people who wrote their own answer, 22 described dynamic constructs, decorators, metaprogramming, or framework behavior. Ten described arrays, dataframes, or scientific typing, and at least eight described annotations that were inaccurate, incomplete, or too broad. Respondents repeatedly named Django, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, and Polars. “Django does so much black magic it’s a wonder a type checker works at all.” — survey respondent Library maintainers need annotations that capture how frameworks and data-science libraries behave. The Pyrefly team has been working with Quansight to improve third-party library typing, including contributions to pandas-stubs and NumPy. Frequency of use changed which problems stood out. Among developers who used type hints rarely or sometimes, 41.6% found the type system too complex or verbose. The rate was 14.5% among developers who used type hints often or always. Missing library typing affected 36.2% of the lower-frequency group and 70.0% of the higher-frequency group. “I use the straightforward parts and avoid the parts that are difficult to understand.” — survey respondent. Years of typing experience showed a different pattern. Complexity was reported by 18.2% of respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 16.0% with three to six years, and 21.0% with seven or more. Newer typing users were often regular users and experienced Python developers: Of the 396 respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 306 (77.3%) used type hints often or always and 345 (87.1%) had used Python for at least three years. Guidance for developers who are new to typing should assume Python experience and show how to add types to an existing repository. Occasional users need a useful first check with little configuration and easy-to-understand errors. As we change the type system, we should aim to support more patterns without making common tasks harder. Better Callable syntax is one practical place to start. It was the most selected missing feature, chosen by 45.7% of the 1,486 respondents who answered the question. The selection rate was similar for respondents who reported complexity and the rest of the sample. Newer Checkers Gained Ground Quickly Frequent type hint use remained between 85.5% and 88.0% across the three surveys: 88.0% in 2024, 85.9% in 2025, and 85.5% in 2026. A different group answered each year, but the overall rate remained consistent. Checker choice was far less stable. When the 2024 Python Typing survey asked what feature was missing from the Python type system, one response now reads like a preview of the changes captured in this year’s results: “A faster Mypy. Its lack of speed led to ecosystem fracturing and other type checkers don’t support Mypy plugins and behave differently in general.” – survey respondent By 2026, developers had several newer open-source checkers to choose from. Speed or performance topped the reasons for choosing a checker, at 56.5%. Using the same list of checkers in both years, 49.9% selected two or more in 2026, up from 46.0% in 2025. Pyrefly is developed by Meta. Respondents could select more than one checker, so the percentages may overlap. Developers Mix Checkers Across Their Workflows Of the 700 respondents who selected Mypy, 297 also selected its editor plugin. Another 314 selected a different named checker integration without selecting the Mypy plugin. Most Pyrefly respondents also selected another checker: 220 of 264, or 83.3%. In the free-text responses, developers described why their teams divide work between checkers: “Because my team members use different IDEs, we use multiple type checkers for development, but rely on Mypy for linting (local and CI).” — survey respondent “Locally we primarily use Pyright because it’s the only option we’ve tried that fully understands all the more niche typing patterns within our codebase. In CI/CD, we do a Pyrefly run and only run Pyright on files where Pyrefly fails, to improve performance of the check.” — survey respondent Among the 1,486 developers who answered the question about difficulties, 33.3% reported inconsistencies between checkers. Among the 738 respondents who selected multiple static checkers and answered the difficulty question, 315 (42.7%) reported inconsistencies between checkers. IDE Support Remains Central as Typing Help Moves Away From Stack Overflow Readability or documentation was the most selected reason to use type hints, chosen by 93.6% of 1,571 respondents. Editor support also ranked highly: 84.8% of the 1,494 people who gave it a numeric rating chose 4 or 5. About 39% of the 103 developers who supplied their own reason mentioned completion, navigation, hover information, or editor error messages. “Drastically improves IDE tooltip/autocomplete.” – survey respondent Real-time editor feedback was widespread: 82.9% of 1,517 respondents ran a type checker in an editor. VS Code was the most selected editor or IDE, at 59.3%. Where developers look for help has changed as well. From 2024 to 2026, Stack Overflow use fell from 46.4% to 22.9%, while large language model (LLM) chat rose from 26.0% to 41.7%. Python typing documentation rose from 56.2% to 65.9%. Checker-specific documentation ended at 60.5%, up from 52.2% after a dip in 2025. General Python documentation fell from 66.7% to 62.2%. As developers move from Stack Overflow to typing- and checker-specific documentation, the quality of those sources matters more. Error messages should link to short, relevant explanations and examples. Links to documentation would also give LLM chat tools better information to work with. It was developed with support from the Pyrefly team at Meta, the PyCharm team at JetBrains, the Python team at Microsoft, the ty team at Astral/OpenAI, and community contributors on discuss.python.org. We shared it through Reddit, X, Mastodon, newsletters, the Python typing forum, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Discord, Slack, and type-checker project websites and social accounts. We lightly edited quotations for spelling, grammar, and punctuation. We thank everyone who responded, shared the survey, reviewed the data, or contributed to the Python typing community. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)
summary: A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice. Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo. The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future. The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon). Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer. The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge. Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week. Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural. AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33. New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3. Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting. Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials. Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality. How U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link. title: [Kubernetes] Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group
summary: We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on. Why workloads need a shared standardCertified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use. Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions. Even so, every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support. A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from. What the working group will deliverThe charter sets out three deliverables: A specification of workload behavior for each Kubernetes minor version. A method for testing each requirement against a running workload. Upstream conformance tooling that implements those tests. The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers. The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn't yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification. The specification covers how a workload runs, and importantly not what it does. Consequently, application logic is out of scope of workload conformance. The binary won't retest anything Certified Kubernetes already covers, and it won't require a particular workload packaging format, or vendor tool like policy engine, security scanner, etc. How the work is organizedTwo Special Interest Groups (SIGs) are sponsors for the working group. SIG Architecture will own the specification and tooling through a subproject, which will be created once the first artifacts are proposed by the Working Group. SIG Apps will bring the application perspective. Whenever a requirement touches another Kubernetes SIG's area, such as node behavior or networking, the working group will initiate conversations with those SIGs as well. The working group is a forum where SIGs can get involved and shape the direction of Workload Conformance while the specification is being written. We're aiming for a stable first specification and working tests within two to three Kubernetes release cycles. Get involvedThe specification will and needs to be built from real examples, so we want to hear your experiences. If you run clusters, tell us how you assess workloads today and what broke during your last upgrade or maintenance window. If you maintain an application, tell us what it needs from the cluster and where the existing guidance left you guessing. Beyond examples, the work needs reviewers for proposed requirements and contributors to write the tests and tooling. When early versions of the tests are ready, we also want early testers to run the binary against your own workloads and tell us where the results differ between runs or environments. If a requirement touches your SIG's area, help us check its scope and the test behind it. And because the subproject will outlive the working group, we're also looking for people who want to maintain it for the long term. You can find us in #wg-workload-conformance on Kubernetes Slack (visit slack.k8s.io for an invitation) and on the mailing list. The working group meets every other Wednesday at 15:00 UTC. The Zoom link and the agenda are in the meeting notes. If you want to raise a topic, add it to the agenda. Joining the mailing list usually adds the meeting invite to your calendar. Thanks to everyone who reviewed and supported the working group proposal.

title: [Kubernetes] Why Is My Kubernetes Job Still Pending? Tracing Kueue Admission with Headlamp
summary: You submit a Kubernetes Job and wait for its Pods to appear. A minute passes. Then another. The Job is still suspended, there are no application logs, and there may not even be a Pod to inspect. In a cluster managed by Kueue, this can be completely normal. Kueue may still be deciding whether the Job can use the requested resources. The useful question is not only “Why is the Pod pending?” It is first “Has Kueue admitted the Workload?” The Kueue plugin for Headlamp brings that investigation into the Headlamp UI. Instead of reconstructing the admission path from several commands and large YAML objects, you can begin with the Workload, read its condition message, and follow links through the LocalQueue, ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Cohort. This article follows that Headlamp-first path. The command line appears only in a short optional section for reproducing the example. Before you beginYou need a Kubernetes cluster with Kueue installed, a Headlamp installation, and the 0.1.0-alpha Kueue plugin. Your Kubernetes identity must be allowed to read the Kueue resources used in this article. The alpha release provides read-only views for Kueue v1beta2 Cohorts, ClusterQueues, LocalQueues, ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions allow them. First, separate admission from Pod schedulingKueue and the Kubernetes scheduler answer different questions. Kueue admission: Should this Workload start now, considering queue policy, quota, ResourceFlavors, admission checks, and other waiting Workloads? Pod scheduling: After the Workload is admitted and the Job resumes, which nodes can run its Pods? That boundary changes the investigation. If the Workload is not admitted, stay in the Kueue section of Headlamp. If it is admitted but its Pods are still Pending, move to Headlamp's normal Job and Pod views and inspect scheduler events. Kueue admission architecture The Headlamp-first troubleshooting pathThe quickest investigation starts with the Workload, not with a shell. Tracing a pending Job through Headlamp Step 1: Open the Workloads viewIn Headlamp, open Kueue → Workloads. Select the namespace that contains the Job, then find the Workload created for it. Kueue creates a Workload to represent the resource request and admission state of a Job. In the alpha plugin, owner references are shown as Kind/name text but are not yet clickable. The Workload name normally contains the Job name, so the namespace filter and table search are the simplest ways to locate it. Before opening the detail page, the list already gives you a useful first scan: LocalQueue priority and priority class active state admitted state completion state a readable current status such as Admitted, Finished, or Inadmissible age If there is no matching Workload, check three things before going further: the selected namespace, whether the Job was submitted to a LocalQueue, and whether your Kubernetes account can list Workloads. The plugin performs permission checks and displays an access message when the current identity cannot read a resource. Step 2: Read status, conditions, and eventsOpen the Workload. Start with its current status and conditions, not with the full YAML. For admission troubleshooting, the most important condition types are QuotaReserved and Admitted. Admitted=True means Kueue has admitted the Workload. The Job can resume, so any remaining Pending Pods belong to the scheduling branch of the investigation. QuotaReserved=False with a reason such as Pending means Kueue has not reserved quota. The condition message explains what prevented the reservation. An Inadmissible status means the Workload currently cannot fit the available queue configuration. A missing covered resource, unsuitable ResourceFlavor, stopped queue, or admission check can all lead you here. For example, a condition message may report that Kueue could not assign a ResourceFlavor because the ClusterQueue has insufficient CPU quota. That message is the first real answer to “Why is my Job still pending?” The rest of the Headlamp journey explains the configuration behind it. Also check the Events section. Conditions describe the current state; events help show what recently changed or what Kueue attempted. Step 3: Compare the Workload's request with its assignmentStay on the Workload detail page and inspect the PodSets and resource requests. The plugin shows the requested Pod count, CPU, memory, and other resources that Kueue evaluates together. This matters because a Job with parallelism: 3 and a one-CPU request per Pod asks Kueue for three CPUs in total. Looking at only one Pod's template would underestimate the Workload. If quota has already been reserved, the same page also shows the assigned ClusterQueue, ResourceFlavors, and admitted resource usage. If those admission assignments are absent, the Workload has not reached that point yet. In our example, the Workload requests: three Pods three CPUs in total 600 MiB of memory in total The next question is where that request entered Kueue. Step 4: Follow the linked LocalQueueUse the LocalQueue link on the Workload detail page. A LocalQueue is the namespace-level entry point used by the Job. It connects namespaced Workloads to a cluster-scoped ClusterQueue. The LocalQueue page shows: its namespace and connected ClusterQueue stop policy and current status pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events related Workloads in the same namespace This page answers two practical questions: Did the Job enter the queue you expected, and is it the only Workload waiting there? If the LocalQueue is inactive or stopped, that may already explain the wait. If it is active, follow the linked ClusterQueue to inspect the capacity behind it. Step 5: Inspect ClusterQueue capacity and usageA ClusterQueue represents the cluster-level quota and admission policy available to one or more LocalQueues. On its Headlamp detail page, compare the Workload request with: covered resources nominal quota for each ResourceFlavor current reservations and usage borrowing and lending limits pending, reserving, and admitted Workload counts queueing strategy and stop policy preemption, fair-sharing, flavor-fungibility, and admission-check settings Kueue conditions and Kubernetes events For the example in this article, the ClusterQueue provides a nominal quota of two CPUs and two Pod slots. The Workload asks for three of each. The condition message and the ClusterQueue page now tell the same story: the Workload does not fit, so Kueue leaves the Job suspended. This is an admission-capacity problem. It is not evidence that kube-scheduler failed to find a node. Step 6: Check ResourceFlavor and Cohort when neededQuota is not always a single pool. A ResourceFlavor can represent a class of compute through node labels, taints, tolerations, or topology settings. Use the ResourceFlavor link from the ClusterQueue when the condition mentions flavor assignment or when the Workload requires a particular hardware class, such as GPU nodes. If the ClusterQueue belongs to a Cohort, follow that link too. Cohorts let ClusterQueues share unused quota. The Headlamp page shows parent and child Cohorts, member ClusterQueues, referenced ResourceFlavors, resource groups, borrowing and lending limits, and fair-sharing information. These pages help answer a more subtle question: Is the Workload blocked because the queue has no quota of its own, because it cannot borrow enough, or because no suitable flavor can be assigned? What we learned without leaving HeadlampFor the sample pending Job, the UI gives us a complete explanation: The Workload is not admitted. Its QuotaReserved condition is false and the message points to insufficient quota. The Workload requests three CPUs and three Pod slots. Its LocalQueue is active and points to the expected ClusterQueue. The ClusterQueue provides only two CPUs and two Pod slots. Kueue therefore keeps the Job suspended until quota becomes available or the queue configuration changes. The important part is not that Headlamp invents a new status. It reads the same Kubernetes API objects as other clients, then places the related resources and human-readable values in one connected investigation. If the Workload is admitted, switch viewsSuppose the Workload detail page shows Admitted=True, but the application is still not running. Kueue has completed its part of the decision. Continue in Headlamp's standard Kubernetes views: Open Workloads → Jobs and inspect the Job state and events. Open Workloads → Pods and filter by the Job name or namespace. Select a Pending Pod and read its Events section. At this stage, look for scheduler concerns such as insufficient node capacity, node affinity, taints and tolerations, topology constraints, persistent-volume binding, or image-pull failures. This handoff is the most useful troubleshooting rule in the article: Not admitted: investigate Kueue resources in Headlamp. Admitted, but Pods are Pending: investigate Job, Pod, node, and scheduler information in Headlamp. A repeatable Headlamp checklistWhen the next Job does not start, use this short path: Open Kueue → Workloads and select the correct namespace. Find the Workload associated with the Job. Check the readable status, Admitted, and QuotaReserved conditions. Read the condition message and recent events. Compare PodSet resource requests with any admission assignments. Follow the LocalQueue link and confirm its status and ClusterQueue. Follow the ClusterQueue link and compare quota, reservations, usage, and policy. Inspect ResourceFlavor or Cohort details when the message points to flavor selection or shared quota. If admitted, move to Headlamp's Job and Pod views. What Headlamp replaces during this investigationThe plugin does not replace kubectl or kueuectl for scripts, exact object output, or changes. It replaces the repetitive UI-less navigation needed during an interactive investigation. Question Headlamp path Command-line equivalent Is the Workload admitted? Kueue → Workloads → status and conditions kubectl describe workload <workload-name> -n <namespace> Which LocalQueue did it enter? Workload → linked LocalQueue kubectl get localqueue <localqueue-name> -n <namespace> -o yaml Which ClusterQueue provides quota? LocalQueue → linked ClusterQueue kubectl get clusterqueue <clusterqueue-name> -o yaml Which flavor or shared quota matters? ClusterQueue → ResourceFlavor or Cohort kubectl get resourceflavor <flavor-name> -o yaml or kubectl get cohort <cohort-name> -o yaml What happened after admission? Workloads → Jobs and Pods → events kubectl describe job <job-name> -n <namespace> or kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> For scripts and GitOps workflows, the command line remains the right tool. For a person asking “why is this waiting?”, the linked Headlamp path is usually faster to read. Optional: reproduce the pending scenarioThe plugin repository includes sample Cohort, ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, ResourceFlavor, and Job manifests for local testing. Apply those examples to a cluster where Kueue is installed, then open the Kueue section in Headlamp. To reproduce the specific quota mismatch used in this article, configure a ClusterQueue with two CPUs and two Pod slots, then submit a three-Pod Job that requests one CPU per Pod. The Job enters its LocalQueue, Kueue creates a Workload, and the Workload remains pending because the combined request is larger than the available quota. Keeping this setup separate from the main walkthrough is intentional: once the resources exist, the investigation itself should happen in Headlamp. Current alpha limitationsThe 0.1.0-alpha release is an initial read-only view of the Kueue admission path. The plugin does not add its own create, edit, pause, resume, or delete flows. Workload owner references are displayed as text and are not currently navigable. The UI depends on the Kubernetes permissions of the identity used by Headlamp. Metrics and a visual relationship map are possible follow-up areas rather than features of this release. These limits are useful to state clearly: the plugin's current purpose is to make admission state and resource relationships easier to inspect. Developed during LFX MentorshipThe plugin was developed during CNCF LFX Mentorship 2026 Term 2 using TypeScript, React, Kubernetes APIs, and Headlamp's plugin system. Utkarsh Raj implemented the plugin with guidance and review from René Dudfield (@illume) and Kevin Hannon (@kannon92). Feedback from the Headlamp and Kueue communities shaped the resource views, status presentation, navigation, documentation, tests, and first alpha release. Try it and share feedbackExplore the plugin source and README, read the 0.1.0-alpha release documentation, or share feedback in the release issue. If a pending Workload is still difficult to explain after following the Headlamp path, that is exactly the kind of feedback that can improve the plugin.

title: [Kubernetes] The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
summary:
In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources. Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers, ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other. With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into maintenance mode. Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25. Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy, a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation and modern resource-management features. Deprecation of cgroup v1Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1. Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the kubelet configuration file, but removal will follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy. Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support. If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup. For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators, returns an error during kubeadm init, kubeadm join, and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details. The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks, and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2. Limitations of cgroup v1 and Improvements with cgroup v2The Linux kernel documentation describes both interfaces: cgroup v1 documentation cgroup v2 documentation Let's enumerate some known issues. active_file memory is not considered available memoryThe kubelet treats active_file memory as not reclaimable. For I/O-intensive workloads, a large page cache can therefore make the kubelet report memory pressure and evict Pods. This is a known kubelet issue (kubernetes/kubernetes#43916); migrating to cgroup v2 does not by itself change that calculation. The documented workaround is to set equal memory requests and limits for containers that perform intensive I/O, after measuring an appropriate value. Memory QoS updates in Kubernetes v1.36Memory QoS was introduced as an alpha feature in Kubernetes v1.22 and updated in v1.27. It remains alpha in v1.36, but now separates memory throttling from memory reservation and adds tiered memory protection: Memory QoS is available only on Linux nodes that use cgroup v2. It relies on the cgroup v2 memory controller: memory.high provides throttling, while memory.min and memory.low provide hard and soft protection when tiered reservation is enabled. cgroup v1 cannot provide this protection model. Enabling the MemoryQoS feature gate applies memory.high throttling to Burstable containers. The threshold is derived from the request, limit, and memoryThrottlingFactor (default 0.9). memoryReservationPolicy: None is the default. It does not write memory.min or memory.low. memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation maps Guaranteed Pod memory requests to memory.min (hard protection) and Burstable Pod requests to memory.low (soft protection). BestEffort Pods receive neither protection. The kubelet exposes Alpha metrics for the total memory.min and memory.low reservations on a node. Kernel 5.9 or later is recommended. On older kernels, memory.high reclaim can trigger a known livelock; from v1.36 the kubelet logs a warning when Memory QoS is enabled on an affected kernel. For example, to opt in to tiered protection: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration featureGates: MemoryQoS: true memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation memoryThrottlingFactor: 0.9 The overall Kubernetes recommendation is not to enable Alpha features in production; however, if you judge that memory QoS with tiered reservations is useful for your platform in production, make sure to test the configuration and account for hard-reserved memory before you enable the TieredReservation feature gate. See the Pod QoS documentation for the current mapping of Kubernetes QoS classes to cgroup v2 controls. Container-aware OOM handlingOn cgroup v2 nodes, the kubelet defaults singleProcessOOMKill to false. It therefore sets memory.oom.group for each container cgroup so that an OOM event kills all processes in that container together, rather than leaving a partially functioning multi-process container. Set singleProcessOOMKill: true only if you need the cgroup v1-compatible behavior where the kernel may kill one process at a time. See the KubeletConfiguration reference for this setting. This behavior is scoped to a container cgroup, not the whole Pod. Also, cgroup.kill is a separate administrative interface: writing 1 to it sends SIGKILL to every process in that cgroup and its descendants; it does not configure OOM behavior. The cgroup v2 memory controller additionally provides memory.events counters that monitoring systems and userspace OOM managers can observe. Rootless supportIn cgroup v1, delegating controllers to less privileged containers may be dangerous. Unlike cgroup v1, cgroup v2 officially supports delegation. Most implementations of rootless containers rely on systemd for delegating v2 controllers to non-root users. This delegation mechanism is separate from Kubernetes Pod user namespaces, which map container users to unprivileged host users. Pod user namespace support graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.36; check its filesystem, kernel, CRI runtime, and OCI runtime prerequisites before enabling it. What else? eBPF stories: In cgroup v1, device access controls are exposed through interface files. The cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files, and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF. Cilium attaches BPF cgroup programs for socket-based load balancing. Its default cgroup root is /run/cilium/cgroupv2. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) reports CPU, memory, and I/O contention at node, Pod, and container level. On supported clusters, the kubelet exposes PSI by default (KubeletPSI is stable and locked on). PSI requires cgroup v2, Linux 4.20 or later, CONFIG_PSI=y, and a kernel not booted with psi=0. The kubelet surfaces the data through the Summary API and /metrics/cadvisor. When migrating, update software that reads the cgroup filesystem directly. The migration guidance recommends cAdvisor v0.43.0 or later and lists compatible Java, Node.js, and automaxprocs versions. CPU weight conversion in newer OCI runtimescgroup v1 uses cpu.shares, whereas cgroup v2 uses cpu.weight. Newer OCI runtimes use an improved non-linear conversion that preserves the default priority and gives small CPU requests more usable granularity. The change is implemented in the OCI runtime rather than Kubernetes: it is available in crun v1.23 and runc v1.3.2. After upgrading a runtime, monitoring or policy tools that predict exact cpu.weight values may need updates. Read New Conversion from cgroup v1 CPU Shares to v2 CPU Weight for the formula, examples, and compatibility considerations. In-place resource updatesIn-place Pod vertical scaling graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.35. Kubernetes v1.36 then  (/blog/2026/04/30/kubernetes-v1-36-inplace-pod-level-resources-beta/) in-place vertical scaling for Pod-level resources by default, as a Beta feature. The kubelet coordinates changes between the Pod-level and container cgroups so that increases create headroom before container limits grow, while decreases constrain containers before shrinking the Pod-level boundary. Accurate aggregate enforcement for this v1.36 feature requires cgroup v2. Adopting cgroup version 2RequirementsHere's what you need to use cgroup v2 with Kubernetes. First up, you need to be using a version of Kubernetes with support for v2 cgroup management; that's been stable since Kubernetes v1.25 and all supported Kubernetes releases include this support. You need at least one Linux node; cgroup is a Linux-only concept Your OS install must run with cgroup v2 enabled The kernel version must be 5.8 or later (5.9 or later is recommended when using memory QoS) The container runtime must support cgroup v2. For example: containerd v1.4 or later supports cgroup v2; use containerd v2.0 or later for automatic cgroup-driver discovery CRI-O v1.20 or later The kubelet and the container runtime must both be configured to use the correct cgroup driver. See Configure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. For now, you can opt back in to use cgroup v1; the Kubernetes project recommends using cgroup v2, but in Kubernetes 1.36 (the current release) the cgroup v1 option remains supported as a fallback. That fallback is scheduled for removal in Kubernetes v1.38. If you are running an older cluster, plan to migrate; if you are setting up a new cluster with Linux nodes, you should prefer cgroup v2. In either case, review both the Kubernetes runtime documentation and (if relevant) the containerd compatibility matrix. kernel updates around cgroup v2When Kubernetes was first announced, in 2014, only v1 cgroup existed. Version 2 cgroup management first appeared in Linux kernel 4.5, released in 2016. In Linux 4.5, the cgroup v2 io, memory, and pids controllers were supported. Linux 4.15 added support for the cgroup v2 cpu controller. Pressure Stall Information (PSI) support began with Linux 4.20. The Kubernetes project does not recommend using cgroup v2 with a Linux kernel older than 5.2 due to lack of cgroup-level task freezer support. Kubernetes documents 5.8 as the minimum kernel version for cgroup v2; the root cgroup's system-level cpu.stat file was added in Linux 5.8. The memory.high livelock fix used by Memory QoS is present in Linux 5.9 and later. memory.peak was added in Linux 5.19. cgroup driver configurationConfigure the kubelet's cgroup driver to match the container runtime cgroup driver. If you use kubeadm to manage your cluster, Kubernetes recommends that you use the systemd cgroup driver, because kubeadm manages the kubelet as a systemd service. For other management tooling, check the documentation for the tool you're using to manage your cluster. If you can pick either option, I recommend using the systemd driver. Whatever tooling you've chosen, the kubelet automatically tries to detect the runtime's recommended cgroup driver. This automatic detection relies on using a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (for example: containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). If you're using a container runtime that supports cgroup v2 but doesn't support automatic cgroup driver detection, you can manually configure an override by editing the kubelet configuration file. For example: apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: KubeletConfiguration cgroupDriver: systemd Automatic discovery of the runtime's cgroup driver through the CRI, tracked by KEP-4033, graduated to stable in Kubernetes v1.34. It requires a runtime that implements the RuntimeConfig CRI RPC (containerd v2.0+ or CRI-O v1.28+). When available, the kubelet uses the value reported by the runtime instead of its configured cgroupDriver value. Tools and commands for troubleshootingTools and commands that you should know about cgroups: stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup/: Check whether cgroup v2 is enabled; it returns cgroup2fs. systemctl list-units 'kube*' --type=slice or --type=scope: List Kubernetes-related units that systemd currently has in memory. bpftool cgroup list /sys/fs/cgroup/*: List all programs attached to the cgroup CGROUP. systemd-cgls /sys/fs/cgroup/*: Recursively show control group contents. systemd-cgtop: Show top control groups by their resource usage. tree -L 2 -d /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice: Show Pods' related cgroups directories. How to check if a Pod CPU or memory limit is successfully applied to the cgroup file?Work from the API object down to the node. Identify the node, then compare desired resources in the spec with the enacted values in status (in-place resize can leave those out of sync): kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}{"
"}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .spec.containers}{.name}{" spec	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' kubectl get pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> \ -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses}{.name}{" status	"}{.resources}{"
"}{end}' On that node, as root, with the systemd cgroup driver and cgroup v2 (these snippets also need jq). Pin the container with kubelet labels; a container name alone is not unique on a node. Use crictl ps -a if the container is not running: CONTAINER_ID=$(crictl ps \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.namespace=<namespace> \ --label io.kubernetes.pod.name=<pod-name> \ --name <container-name> -q | head -n1) # OCI view (not the CRI protobuf field names) crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq '.info.runtimeSpec.linux.resources' # Kernel cgroup path for this container PID=$(crictl inspect "$CONTAINER_ID" | jq -r '.info.pid') CGROUP="/sys/fs/cgroup$(awk -F: '$1=="0"{print $3}' /proc/$PID/cgroup)" cat "$CGROUP/cpu.weight" # request.cpu → shares → weight; not a limit cat "$CGROUP/cpu.max" # limit.cpu as "quota period"; unlimited is "max <period>" cat "$CGROUP/memory.max" # limit.memory; unlimited is "max" # Pod-level cgroup (parent slice), used by Pod-level resources cat "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/cpu.max" "$(dirname "$CGROUP")/memory.max" # Present when MemoryQoS is enabled cat "$CGROUP/memory.high" "$CGROUP/memory.min" "$CGROUP/memory.low" SCOPE=$(basename "$CGROUP") systemctl show "$SCOPE" \ -p CPUWeight -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p CPUQuotaPeriodUSec -p MemoryMax Do not treat info.runtimeSpec.linux.cgroupsPath as a filesystem path when the runtime uses the systemd driver; that value is a systemd unit path (slice:runtime:id), not a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup. Expected mapping at each layer: Kubernetes: spec.containers.resources (desired) and status.containerStatuses.resources (enacted after in-place resize). Pod-level resources are on spec.resources and the parent pod slice. CRI (kubelet → runtime; these protobuf names stay cgroup v1-style even on v2): cpu_shares, cpu_quota, cpu_period, memory_limit_in_bytes, plus unified for Memory QoS. crictl inspect does not show these names; it shows the OCI spec the runtime derived from them. OCI spec: linux.resources.cpu.{shares,quota,period}, linux.resources.memory.limit, and linux.resources.unified. The runtime converts shares, quota, and period into cgroup v2 files. After upgrading crun or runc, the shares-to-weight formula may change; see CPU weight conversion. systemd scope: CPUWeight, CPUQuotaPerSecUSec, CPUQuotaPeriodUSec, MemoryMax. Unlimited or unset values often appear as  or infinity. cgroupfs: cpu.weight (from CPU request; an unset request still yields the default of 2 shares), cpu.max, and memory.max on the container scope. Memory QoS adds memory.high, memory.min, and memory.low. title: [Kubernetes] Scaling Kubernetes Workloads with Node Swap
summary: Memory is often the first hard limit a Kubernetes cluster hits. Nodes run out of RAM long before they run out of CPU, and the new wave of agentic AI workloads makes this worse. These workloads demand large memory footprints to start up and run untrusted code, then sit idle waiting for the next prompt. That idle but resident memory is expensive, and it caps how many pods a node can hold. This is where swap helps. Kubernetes support for running nodes with swap enabled reached General Availability in v1.34, and by backing that swap with fast NVMe solid state drives (SSDs), a node can page out dormant memory and pack in far more pods. This post explains how we benchmarked that approach across three workloads, including CI/CD kernel builds, sandboxed headless browsers, and isolated Python runtimes; we found density gains of up to 3×, often with little or no latency cost. The node density problemThe Kubernetes ecosystem has reached a fundamental physical resource constraint: the strict limits of hardware memory versus the growing demand for dynamic, bursty workloads in the new agentic era. Historically, administrators provisioning memory-intensive workloads encountered a persistent dilemma: set memory limits too high and you waste expensive infrastructure on idle RAM; set them too low and you risk Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills. This conflict is amplified when deploying autonomous AI agents using secure execution environments like the agent-sandbox framework. These agentic pods require large memory footprints to initialize and execute untrusted code. However, after their burst of activity, they typically enter long-tail idle phases waiting for user prompts. Keeping this idle state in physical RAM caps cluster density and makes AI infrastructure expensive to run. The solution: Kubernetes node swapWith the introduction of Kubernetes' support for running nodes with swap enabled (which reached General Availability in v1.34), this paradigm shifts. By enabling the Linux kernel to page out anonymous memory to disk, node swap acts as a shock absorber during traffic spikes or periods of heavy memory oversubscription. Historically, swap was discouraged in Kubernetes for two reasons. The first was memory accounting. Under cgroup v1, the controls treated memory and swap as a single combined limit rather than letting operators set an independent limit for disk swap. Without independent tracking, a process could page large amounts of anonymous memory out to disk, which made a container's real memory usage unpredictable and hard to isolate. Kubernetes' swap support resolves this by relying on cgroup v2, whose separate swap accounting tracks disk swap on its own. The second reason was the latency penalty of paging to slow spinning disks, which fast NVMe Local SSDs largely eliminate. Together, these make it practical to increase pod density and buffer against memory spikes without sacrificing cluster stability. The benchmark dataTo quantify the performance boundaries and cost-saving potential of Local SSD-backed node swap, this analysis covers three distinct workload categories: a Traditional Build Workload for CI/CD pipelines, High-Density Browser Sandboxes, and Isolated Python Sandboxes. Workload Profile Baseline Capacity (No Swap) Local SSD Swap Capacity Density Improvement Linux CI/CD Kernel Build 600 MB RAM Limit 300 MB RAM Limit -50% RAM Footprint Headless Chrome (Kata) 40 Concurrent Pods 50 Concurrent Pods +25% Pod Density Headless Chrome (gVisor) 80 Concurrent Pods 160 Concurrent Pods +100% Pod Density Python Sandbox (gVisor) 80 Concurrent Pods 240 Concurrent Pods +200% Pod Density 1. Traditional workload: Linux kernel buildBefore exploring specialized agentic architectures, swap was validated against classic batch workloads by running a complete Linux 6.1.1 kernel build. The kernel compilation process leverages concurrent worker threads, balloons in memory to hold compiled object files, and requires a large memory spike during the brief linking phase. This workload mirrors the memory behavior of enterprise CI/CD pipelines. Because earlier compiled objects sit inactive in memory while the pipeline progresses, CI/CD jobs frequently hoard unused physical RAM, which makes them well suited to node swap compression. On a baseline node without swap, the minimum memory limit to prevent an OOM crash during compilation was 600 MB. Routing swap to a Local SSD cut the container memory limit by 50% to 300 MB without incurring any execution slowdown (in fact, it ran cleanly in 374s vs the baseline 433s). However, as an explicit tradeoff, compressing the limit further to 200 MB forced the active working set into swap, causing long I/O wait times and increasing execution time by over 40%. This reinforces that swap serves as an insurance policy for burst memory, not a replacement for active RAM. 2. High-density agent workloads: headless browser runtimesAI agent workloads frequently require manipulating headless browsers via Chromium. However, trusting external code execution often requires stricter security isolation than standard Linux namespaces. This benchmark cross-evaluated several container runtime environments. The raw logs and testing methodologies for the default runtime are available in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap directory. Unsandboxed baseline limits (runc): To test the limits of the environment without the overhead of security runtimes, plain runc containers were swept on a c4-standard-32 node (32 vCPU, 120 GB RAM). Without swap, the node exhausted physical memory and failed past 512 pods. Enabling Local SSD swap allowed the node to support 768 concurrent pods. Advanced security runtimes (for example: gVisor, Kata Containers): Enabling strict security sandboxing increases memory overhead and normally reduces pod density. However, memory swap naturally absorbs this overhead penalty. Without swap, a gVisor environment hit a hard limit at 80 pods. Local SSD swap doubled that capacity, which allowed 160 concurrent gVisor pods on a single node. Similarly, Kata Containers microVMs exhausted physical RAM at 40 concurrent pods without swap, but using GCP Local SSD swap expanded this to 50 stable Kata microVMs before CPU saturation. At these maximum densities, the per-pod latency increase is driven mainly by pods competing for CPU, not by swap I/O. An operator tuning for a specific latency target would run at a lower density than the peak numbers here and see a proportionally smaller latency cost. For a comprehensive architectural breakdown and density metrics for gVisor and Kata, see the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap Runtimes directory. 3. Beyond browsers: sandboxed Python runtimesThe advantages of node swap also extend to untrusted, isolated code-execution environments. This sweep deployed simultaneous Python sandbox sessions analyzing 5 million rows of data from the MovieLens 20M dataset, requiring a ≃375 MiB resident memory footprint per execution. The in-depth scaling results and deployment code for this sweep can be reviewed in the Agent Sandbox GKE Swap Python Density directory. Without swap, heavy concurrent bursts exhausted physical memory, causing the node to hit a hard RAM limit and fail at 80 concurrent sessions. Enabling Local SSD swap offloaded dormant anonymous memory, freeing up physical RAM and preserving the node's page cache. This allowed the node to scale to 240 concurrently isolated Python sandboxes—a 3× density improvement. As with the browser workloads, the latency rise at peak density comes mainly from the sandboxes competing for CPU rather than from swap itself. Density Benchmarks with and without Node Swap How to use itIf you manage Kubernetes infrastructure for developer environments, browser testing farms, JVM applications, or AI execution runtimes, leveraging Local SSD swap can multiply your density efficiency. In Kubernetes v1.34+, node swap is Generally Available. You enable it via the kubelet configuration: kind: KubeletConfiguration apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 failSwapOn: false memorySwap: swapBehavior: LimitedSwap Pairing this upstream configuration with your cloud provider's high-speed local disk gives you dynamic memory balancing. For example, this is natively supported on Google Kubernetes Engine via Node Memory Swap configured on Local SSD profiles. To get the benefits, configure your workloads with Burstable QoS: set your container's memory limits higher than its requests. The node automatically rations fast swap space based on idle application memory usage while keeping active processes responsive. ConclusionAs the Kubernetes ecosystem transitions into the agentic era, administrators face a growing conflict between finite hardware memory limits and the bursty behavior of AI workloads. Frameworks like Agent Sandbox provide the security isolation required for running untrusted agents, but that isolation traditionally demands large amounts of idle memory overhead. By configuring the kubelet with LimitedSwap and routing it to Local SSDs, you can mitigate this conflict. Fast swap offloads the dormant states of idle agents, allowing you to increase pod density and node utilization on the same infrastructure without compromising security boundaries.

title: [CNCF] The Linkerd Story: The People Behind The Service Mesh — A new documentary premieres at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026
summary: Join CNCF and Buoyant on November 9 in Salt Lake City for the premiere of a new documentary celebrating a decade of Linkerd, the evolution of service mesh technology, and the people who helped make it possible. Every open source project has a story. Behind the code are people with ideas, challenges to overcome, decisions to make, and a shared belief that technology can be better when built together. This November, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), in partnership with Buoyant, is excited to premiere The Linkerd Story: The People Behind The Service Mesh, a new documentary exploring the origins, evolution, and community behind one of cloud native’s pioneering open source projects. From the engineering challenges of Twitter’s early infrastructure to the creation of the first service mesh, the documentary takes viewers behind the scenes of Linkerd’s journey, told through the experiences of the creators, maintainers, contributors, and end users who have helped shape it. This documentary explores a story beyond technology. It’s about the relationships, persistence, and collective effort that turn an idea into an open source project used by organizations around the world. From an engineering challenge to a pioneering open source project Linkerd’s story begins at Twitter, where engineers were tackling the challenges of running increasingly complex distributed systems. Their experiences with Finagle, a library for managing communication between services, helped inspire a new approach to application networking. That approach became Linkerd, helping establish the service mesh category and changing how teams could manage reliability, security, and observability across distributed applications. The documentary explores the technical decisions that shaped the project, including its evolution into a Kubernetes-focused service mesh, the adoption of Rust for lightweight sidecar proxies, and the ongoing challenge of making complex infrastructure simpler to operate. Through firsthand accounts, viewers discover the experimentation, challenges, and collaboration behind these milestones. The people who make open source possible At the heart of the documentary is the Linkerd community. Contributors share stories of friendships, shared challenges, and the responsibility that comes with building technology organizations depend on. The film highlights the role of maintainers, ambassadors, and end users in helping the project grow, from contributing code and documentation to sharing knowledge and supporting others. It also explores Linkerd’s journey to becoming a CNCF graduated project and the importance of open governance, collaboration, and long-term sustainability. The documentary brings these themes to life through real-world experiences, including how Texas-based grocery retailer H-E-B used Linkerd while accelerating the rollout of its curbside services. These stories demonstrate that the impact of open source extends beyond technology, reaching the people and communities who depend on the systems it helps power. Ten years of Linkerd, and looking ahead As Linkerd marks a decade of development, the documentary reflects on what it takes to build an open source project that lasts. One contributor shares an ambition for Linkerd to continue for another hundred years, a reminder that long-term success depends not only on technical innovation but also on the people who sustain it. It’s a theme that reflects CNCF’s mission to support sustainable, community-driven cloud native projects. Join us for the documentary premiere We’re excited to share this story with the cloud native community at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. Presented by CNCF in partnership with Buoyant, The Linkerd Story: The People Behind The Service Mesh offers a behind-the-scenes look at the people, decisions, and experiences that helped shape a decade of service mesh innovation. Premiere details Date: Monday, November 9, 2026 Time: 6:30 PM MST Location: Salt Palace Convention Center | Level 1 | Room 151 Event: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 Whether you’ve contributed to Linkerd, used it in production, or are curious about the people behind cloud native innovation, we invite you to join us for this special premiere. Come celebrate the people behind the service mesh. We look forward to seeing you in Salt Lake City! Learn more about Linkerd and explore the CNCF project landscape.

title: [CNCF] KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026: End User TAB recommendations and tips
summary: KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City will bring the cloud native community together with projects, vendors and end users in what is one of the largest open source events. In this post, we highlight content specifically targeted at end users and session recommendations from members of the CNCF End User Technical Advisory Board (TAB), along with practical tips for making the most of the event. Birds of Feather (BoF) Newly introduced at Kubecon EU in Amsterdam back in March, we will again have a series of BoF sessions in Salt Lake City. Last time we had packed rooms discussing and brainstorming around AI infrastructure and platforms, AI observability and optimized infrastructure for training, inference and GPU efficiency. This time around we’ll open the floor to our newly formed end user groups, the TAB recently approved end user groups covering Platform Engineering, Public Sector, Telecom and Research. And in another session we will give ourselves a challenge: get end users in one room and try to build live a reference architecture for Agentic AI deployments. It’s not clear how far we will get given how fast things are moving and how different use cases can be… but it should be a good learning session and it will definitely be fun! Town Hall In Amsterdam we chose to move the End User TAB Town Hall to the project pavilion and that was well received. So we’re keeping it this way and you can come and ask us questions right next to where the projects are located. Poster sessions Did you know Kubecon has a poster session? It’s an ideal setting to have more in-depth discussions with the authors and there are several end user focused presentations this time around.
